country.comment: Study examines water governance in the São Francisco River Integration Project (PISF) in the Semiárido region of Brazil, focusing on the Agreste and Sertão microregions of Pernambuco (and interconnected basins in Paraíba, Ceará, and Rio Grande do Norte).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Affiliations; PDF p. 2, Introdução; PDF pp. 9–12, Resultados da Pesquisa

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative institutional analysis using Ostrom's IAD framework; descriptive institutional/operational figures reported in text (e.g., 50% Union-plus-four-states bloc in SGIB, 20% civil society share, 62 CBHSF members, 10 m³/s vs 28 m³/s East Axis flow), with no statistical effect estimate.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Applying Ostrom's IAD framework to the São Francisco River Integration Project (PISF), the study finds that territorial and institutional fragmentation across federal and state agencies (MI, ANA, Codevasf, DNOCS, Compesa, APAC), centralized decision-making (the Union and four states form a 50% majority bloc in SGIB, while civil society and key actors hold 20% in CNRH-subordinated governance), and power and information asymmetries silence local, quilombola, and indigenous communities (such as the Pipipã) and render formal participation largely symbolic. Although water is retained and the East Axis operates at a continuous flow of 10 m³/s (out of 28 m³/s designed capacity), water distribution remains unequal (favoring localities with purchasing power and sanitary infrastructure), secondary supply networks and strategic reservoirs suffer from obsolescence and management failures causing supply collapses, and boundary and enforcement rules governing access to transposed waters (including canals crossing private properties, diffuse uses, and tariff-conditioned pumping) are fragile despite Law 9.433/1997.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 1–2, Resumo/Abstract; PDF pp. 10–12, Resultados da Pesquisa; PDF pp. 12–15, Discussão dos resultados; PDF pp. 15–16, Considerações Finais

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 for a primary qualitative study (CASP). Rated 2 because the authors directly empirically document the institutional and administrative mechanisms (intergovernmental fragmentation, centralized SGIB/CNRH decision rules, symbolic participation, tariff-conditioned pumping authorization, and weak boundary/access enforcement along canals) operating on water distribution and supply outcomes via primary interviews (2015–2018), field research, and regulatory/audit documents.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 8–9, Metodologia; PDF pp. 9–15, Resultados da Pesquisa & Discussão dos resultados

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines intergovernmental and agency fragmentation and overlapping mandates (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination), asymmetric participatory arenas in CBHSF/SGIB/CNRH (participation), water-use rights and canals crossing private lands vs indigenous views of water (property), basin/infrastructure planning under Singreh/EIA (planning), state tariffs/charges conditioning authorization to pump transposed water (fees), and fragile boundary monitoring/enforcement and payoff sanction rules over water withdrawals (sanction).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, property, planning, fees, sanction, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 1–2, Resumo/Abstract; PDF pp. 7–8, Tabela 1; PDF pp. 9–12, Resultados da Pesquisa; PDF pp. 13–15, Discussão dos resultados

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes unequal access to transposed water and arrival of water to final consumers (water_access), municipal water supply collapses and reservoir management/regularization failures (service_reliability, service_continuity), and canal flow rates and storage capacity relative to demand (service_quantity).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary qualitative empirical study based on open conversational individual interviews, in loco field observation, and documentary analysis, matched to the CASP Qualitative Checklist per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF pp. 8–9, Metodologia; PDF p. 13, Discussão dos resultados

sample_size.comment: Exact total counts of individual interviewees and analyzed documents are not reported. Within the single PISF governance arena, interviews (2015–2018) included 1 APAC/Prorural representative, 1 Fundaj researcher, 1 Compesa business manager, 1 Codevasf representative, and unspecified numbers of representatives from MI/PISF coordination, the Observatório das Águas (OGA) group, 1 quilombola community (Garanhuns), and 2 indigenous communities (Ibimirim and Pesqueira), alongside documentary sources (EIA, legislation, audit reports).

study_design.comment: Qualitative empirical study applying Ostrom's Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework to the PISF governance arena, combining documentary/regulatory analysis, open conversational individual interviews conducted between 2015 and 2018, and in loco field observation, analyzed using pragmatics of language in NVivo 11.
study_design.value: Qualitative institutional case study (Ostrom's IAD framework using documentary analysis and open conversational individual interviews, 2015–2018)
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Resumo/Abstract; PDF pp. 8–9, Metodologia; PDF p. 13, Discussão dos resultados
